48494.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse ríða (“to ride”), from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną (“to ride”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreydʰ- (“to set in motion, ride”), likely a suffixed form of *h₃reyH- (“to move, churn”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ri, ride, Danish ride, Swedish rida, Icelandic ríða, Faroese ríða, German reiten, Dutch rijden and English ride. / Inherited from Old Norse riða (“to twist; to bind, tie”), from Proto-Germanic *wrīþaną (“to weave, twist”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreyt- (“to twist, writhe”). The nautical sense developed from the older meaning “to twist, bind, tie” to “tighten, lash fast”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk vri (“to twist, turn”), Swedish vrida (“to twist, turn”), Danish vride (“to twist, wring”), Icelandic ríða (“to twist, wind”) and English writhe.

44910.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse pikka (“to hack, prick”), originally imitative of a short tapping or striking sound and traditionally connected with Proto-Germanic *pikkōną (“to pick, peck, prick, knock”). The senses involving birds, light knocking, working with a pointed tool and ticking sounds all continue this sound-symbolic verb.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk pikke, Danish pikke, Swedish picka, Icelandic pikka, Dutch pikken, German picken and English pick (“to pick, peck, prick or tap”). / Borrowed from English pick (“to collect, gather”), especially through the English phrasal verb pick up (“to collect, fetch or acquire”). In Norwegian, this verb occurs especially in the unlinked expression pikke opp. This etymology is distinct from, but ultimately related to, the inherited Germanic verb in Etymology 2.

1004910.etyen:
From blokk (“block”) + undervisning (“teaching, instruction”), literally “block teaching”.
The first element, blokk (“block”), is from Middle Low German block (“block”). Here it is used in its abstract sense of a coherent or continuous unit, referring to teaching being organized into concentrated periods or “blocks”. The second element, undervisning (“teaching, instruction”), is derived from undervise (“to teach”) + -ning.
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk blokkundervising (also blokkundervisning), Danish blokundervisning and Swedish blockundervisning (“block teaching”).

The first element, løk (“bulb, onion”), is traced by Bokmålsordboka to Old Norse laukr (“leek, onion, garlic”), from Proto-Germanic *laukaz (“onion, leek”), of uncertain further origin. NAOB explains the written form through Danish løg and Old Danish løk (“onion”).
